scenario.speaker: marcus
scenario.briefing:
Nice work on SwiftCart and TrailTonic — Dana read both proposals and signed off without edits. So here's your reward: more work.

Three new RFPs landed this morning — **Wagly** (pet wearables), **LumenDesk** (home-office furniture), and **ParkPass** (mobile parking payments). These three are yours. I'm not going to walk you through them the way I did last time; you know the drill by now. Find the decision, classify the evidence, check the constraints.

The RFPs are in your **Inbox** with a short note from me on each. One methodology recommendation per client. The methodology guide is still in **Guides** if you want a refresher — but this time, I'd like the reasoning to be yours before you peek.

inbox.subject: Three RFPs — these are yours
inbox.body:
Wagly, LumenDesk, and ParkPass all came in overnight. I skimmed each one exactly once, and I'm deliberately not telling you what I think.

One piece of advice and then I'll get out of your way: clients rarely name the method they need, but they almost always *describe* it. Words are evidence. When an RFP says it wants to *explore*, *generate*, or *hear reactions*, that's one family of methods. When it says the facts *probably already exist somewhere*, that's another. When it says *measure*, *projectable*, or *statistically representative*, that's a third. Read each RFP twice — once for the business decision, once for the language.

Budgets and timelines still matter. A directionally correct method scoped wrong for the client is still the wrong recommendation.

Send me one methodology per client. I'll review all three before they go out.

— Marcus

inbox.subject: Wagly, Inc. RFP
inbox.body:
First up: Wagly makes collar-mounted health and GPS trackers for dogs. They're committed to building a second-generation device and need to figure out what goes in it. RFP attached — pay attention to what kind of evidence they say they value at this stage.

— Marcus

attachments.title: Request for Proposal — Wagly, Inc.
attachments.body:
**Wagly, Inc. — Request for Proposal**

**Company background.** Wagly designs and sells collar-mounted wearables for dogs that combine health monitoring (activity, sleep, scratching) with GPS location tracking. We sell direct-to-consumer and through specialty pet retailers, with roughly 180,000 active devices in the field. Our first-generation tracker has been on the market for three years.

**Business decision.** Leadership has committed to launching a **second-generation product** next year. Engineering can build far more than we can ship — we must decide which features to develop, which to drop, and how the new device should feel different from the current one.

**Research objectives.** We are seeking a research partner to help us:

- **Explore** how owners actually use — and stop using — the current tracker in daily life, in their own words
- **Generate new feature ideas** for a next-generation device, drawn from owners' real routines and frustrations
- Capture spontaneous **reactions to early feature concepts** our team has drafted (vet-data sharing, multi-pet dashboards, behavior alerts)
- Understand **why** owners upgrade, keep, or abandon pet wearables — the reasons behind the behavior, not just the rates

**Constraints.** Our concepts are still forming, so at this stage we value depth, discussion, and the ability to probe over statistical precision. We need findings within **7 weeks** and have budgeted **$20,000–$25,000**.

**Contact.** P. Vance, VP Product, Wagly, Inc.

inbox.subject: LumenDesk, Inc. RFP
inbox.body:
Second: LumenDesk sells home-office furniture online only, and they're wondering whether to open physical showrooms. Notice what they say about where the answers to their questions probably live.

— Marcus

attachments.title: Request for Proposal — LumenDesk, Inc.
attachments.body:
**LumenDesk, Inc. — Request for Proposal**

**Company background.** LumenDesk is a direct-to-consumer home-office furniture brand — sit-stand desks, task seating, and desk lighting — selling exclusively online since 2019. Growth has been strong, but customer-acquisition costs keep rising, and several competitors have opened physical locations.

**Business decision.** The board must decide within the next quarter whether to invest in **retail showrooms** in select metro areas, and if so, what a prudent first phase looks like.

**Research objectives.** We are seeking a research partner to compile and synthesize:

- The size and growth trend of the home-office furniture category, split by online versus brick-and-mortar channels
- **Channel benchmarks**: what share of category sales flows through showrooms, and the typical cost structure of operating one
- The **expansion history of competitors** who moved from online-only to physical retail — what they opened, where, and what happened next, as documented in trade press, industry reports, and public filings
- Established best practices for direct-to-consumer brands entering physical retail

We believe most of these facts have **already been published** across industry and trade sources; the difficulty is finding, verifying, and assembling them into a coherent picture. We are **not seeking new consumer data collection** at this stage.

**Constraints.** Findings needed within **5 weeks**; budget **$12,000–$18,000**. Deliverable: a summary report with a go/no-go recommendation framework.

**Contact.** A. Serrano, CFO, LumenDesk, Inc.

inbox.subject: ParkPass, Inc. RFP
inbox.body:
Third: ParkPass runs a mobile parking-payment app under contract with 40 U.S. cities. Their contracts have a research requirement baked in — read the constraints section carefully.

— Marcus

attachments.title: Request for Proposal — ParkPass, Inc.
attachments.body:
**ParkPass, Inc. — Request for Proposal**

**Company background.** ParkPass operates a mobile parking-payment app under contract with **40 U.S. cities**, serving roughly 2.6 million registered users. Drivers use the app to start, extend, and pay for street and lot parking sessions.

**Business decision.** Our municipal contracts come up for renewal on a rolling basis, and every contract requires us to submit **documented annual measurement of rider satisfaction**. Renewal committees also use these results to weigh service improvements, so the findings feed directly into our product roadmap and pricing discussions with cities.

**Research objectives.** We are seeking a research partner to:

- **Measure** overall rider satisfaction, plus satisfaction with each stage of the parking journey (finding zones, starting a session, payment, extending, receipts and disputes)
- Produce satisfaction scores that are **projectable to our full user base** and reportable **city by city**
- Establish a baseline we can **track year over year** with known statistical precision
- **Quantify** how many users experienced a problem in the past year, and of what type

**Constraints.** Our municipal contracts specify that results must be **statistically representative** of each city's users — measurement precision matters more than exploratory depth. Findings needed within **9 weeks**; budget **$35,000–$45,000**.

**Contact.** T. Iyer, VP Municipal Partnerships, ParkPass, Inc.

guides.title: Rounds 1 & 2 — Choosing a Research Methodology
guides.body:
**Work backward from the client's decision.** Ask: what kind of evidence settles it?

| Method | Typically the right tool when… |
|---|---|
| Secondary research | The facts already exist: market size, competitor landscape, trends, benchmarks |
| Survey | You must *measure* attitudes or behavior and project results to a population |
| Focus groups | You need ideas, language, and reactions — new products, concepts, brainstorming |
| In-depth interviews | Respondents are experts, executives, or the topic is complex/sensitive |
| Observational research | You need actual behavior (not self-reports): shopping paths, decision moments, layouts |
| Mystery shopping | You're auditing whether protocols and service standards are followed |
| Experiment | You must isolate *cause*: does the new thing outperform the current thing? |

**Then apply the constraints.**

- *Read the client's own language.* Words like **explore**, **generate**, **ideas**, **reactions**, and **why** point qualitative. Words like **already published** and **no new data collection** point secondary. Words like **measure**, **projectable**, **statistically representative**, and **track year over year** point quantitative.
- *Budget & timeline:* a method that fits the question but blows the budget or calendar is still the wrong recommendation.
- *One method rarely does everything.* Each RFP in this round is best served by a single methodology aimed at the client's **primary** objective — resist the urge to answer a side interest they didn't fund.
